paragraphs: This paper asks whether reinforcement learning can be built from learning routines that are only slightly better than guessing. Existing reductions turn reinforcement learning into supervised learning problems, allowing compact predictors to handle large decision processes. The authors weaken the required building block: instead of assuming access to an accurate supervised learner, they assume access to weak learners.

The approach follows the idea of boosting, which combines rough rules into a stronger predictor. Applying this idea to reinforcement learning requires addressing a mathematical obstacle. Standard boosting results concern convex losses, whereas the value of a policy is a non-convex objective. The authors use a non-convex variant of the Frank-Wolfe optimization method to make the reduction work.

They prove sample and running-time bounds that do not explicitly depend on the number of states. Their analysis also improves known bounds for reductions using supervised learning. The contribution is therefore both a weaker learning-oracle assumption and improved theoretical efficiency, rather than an empirical demonstration of a particular agent.
neurips-2022-a-boosting-approach-to-rein.tldr: A boosting-based reduction builds reinforcement learning from weak learners and improves theoretical sample and running-time bounds.

paragraphs: A bandit policy can perform well on average while retaining a substantial chance of a very poor run. This paper studies that distinction through regret: the performance lost while learning which arm to choose. Its concern is heavy-tailed regret risk, specifically the probability of regret growing linearly with the time horizon.

The authors prove that policies achieving instance-dependent logarithmic expected regret must retain a polynomially decaying probability of linear regret. They extend this negative finding to all policies in the instance-dependent consistent class. Thus, the strong instance-specific performance criterion carries a restriction on how quickly severe-outcome probabilities can disappear.

For two arms, they design a simple policy with worst-case expected regret of roughly square-root order and linear-regret probability decreasing exponentially in the square root of the horizon. They prove that tail rate is optimal among policies with worst-case-optimal expected regret, then extend the design and analysis to arbitrary arm counts. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory: worst-case average efficiency and light-tailed regret risk can coexist.
neurips-2022-a-simple-and-optimal-policy.tldr: New bandit policies combine worst-case-optimal expected regret with sharply reduced severe-regret risk, while theory exposes a trade-off with instance-dependent consistency.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks mathematical expressions that explain data. Research on this problem has developed several distinct solution strategies, but individual methods often concentrate on improving only one of them. This paper investigates whether combining strategies can improve both the quality of fitted expressions and the recovery of underlying analytical formulas.

The authors organize the available approaches into five classes: recursive problem simplification, neural-guided search, large-scale pre-training, genetic programming, and linear models. They propose a modular framework that integrates these classes. Modularity matters because it makes hybrid construction a deliberate design choice and supports studying which combinations contribute to performance.

Using SRBench, they evaluate the framework on 252 problems covering known generating expressions and black-box datasets, with both noiseless data and several noise levels. They report state-of-the-art results for expression recovery, fitting accuracy, and accuracy-complexity trade-offs. Extensive combinatorial ablations also support practical guidance about building hybrids for different use cases. The stated contribution combines strong benchmark performance with evidence about how to assemble complementary strategies.
neurips-2022-a-unified-framework-for-dee.tldr: A modular framework combines five symbolic regression strategies and reports state-of-the-art performance across 252 benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary detection aims to locate objects from categories beyond those directly covered by conventional detection supervision. This paper identifies a mismatch in two common sources of weak supervision. CLIP learns from image-text pairs without precise object locations, while image-level labels require additional decisions about which local regions represent the named objects.

The proposed method addresses both sides of that mismatch. It aligns CLIP language embeddings with objects and uses a pseudo-labeling process to obtain high-quality object proposals from image-level supervision. These proposals also help expand the vocabulary during training. A learned weight transfer function connects the two alignment strategies so their complementary strengths can be combined.

On COCO, the approach reaches 36.6 AP50 for novel classes, an absolute improvement of 8.2 over the previous best result reported in the abstract. On LVIS, it exceeds ViLD by 5.0 mask AP for rare categories and 3.4 overall. These findings support the value of making weak supervision more object-specific when transferring broad vocabulary knowledge into localization.
neurips-2022-bridging-the-gap-between-ob.tldr: Object-centric alignment connects CLIP and image-level supervision to improve open-vocabulary detection, including novel and rare categories.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains against the worst distribution in a specified uncertainty set. The choice of that set is therefore central. This paper argues that distances measured in the full high-dimensional data space can produce excessively broad sets, making existing robust methods protect against too many possibilities and underperform.

The proposed Geometric Wasserstein DRO incorporates data geometry into the distance metric. Its motivation is that high-dimensional observations often lie approximately on lower-dimensional manifolds. Accounting for this structure further constrains which distributional changes the optimization considers. The authors derive a broadly applicable approximate optimization algorithm using gradient flow, together with bounds on approximation error and algorithm convergence.

The theory also identifies edge cases in which certain existing DRO methods arise as degenerate versions of the proposed formulation. Experiments across multiple settings with strong distribution shifts report better performance than existing DRO methods and show that the resulting uncertainty set adapts to data geometry. The findings connect robustness to the structure of plausible data variation.
neurips-2022-distributionally-robust-opt.tldr: Geometric Wasserstein DRO uses data geometry to constrain distributional uncertainty and reports improved robustness under strong distribution shifts.

paragraphs: When several players learn simultaneously, a central question is whether their current actions approach a Nash equilibrium. This paper studies last-iterate convergence for extragradient and optimistic gradient methods. Last-iterate guarantees concern the actual current output of learning, making them directly relevant to what an algorithm returns after a fixed number of updates.

The authors prove that both methods, with constant step sizes, achieve an equilibrium gap decreasing at order one over the square root of the number of iterations. The result assumes smooth monotone games and allows each player's action set to be an arbitrary convex set. This extends earlier results that treated only unrestricted Euclidean action spaces.

The main analytical tool is a new measure of equilibrium proximity called the tangent residual. The authors use it, or a slight variant, as a potential function and show that it never increases between consecutive iterates. The resulting rates match existing lower bounds, establishing tight convergence guarantees and resolving the stated open question for constrained games.
neurips-2022-finite-time-last-iterate-co.tldr: Extragradient and optimistic gradient achieve tight last-iterate convergence rates in smooth monotone games with arbitrary convex action sets.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when useful rewards arrive only rarely. Intrinsic rewards address this by encouraging agents to explore even before they receive task rewards. This paper questions what kind of novelty those rewards should recognize: existing state-based measures can emphasize low-level changes and may be less suitable for tasks requiring more abstract skills.

The authors investigate natural language as a way to highlight relevant abstractions in an environment. Their approach extends two competitive intrinsic exploration methods, AMIGo and NovelD, with language-based variants. Directly comparing each extension with its non-linguistic form makes the evaluation focus on whether language adds value to established exploration approaches.

Across 13 challenging tasks from MiniGrid and MiniHack, the language-based variants outperform their original forms by 47–85%. These results provide empirical support for using language to shape the abstractions involved in exploration. The contribution is specifically about improving intrinsic exploration in the evaluated tasks, with language serving as a medium for representing what may be relevant beyond low-level novelty.
neurips-2022-improving-intrinsic-explora.tldr: Language-based extensions of AMIGo and NovelD improve intrinsic exploration performance by 47–85% across 13 MiniGrid and MiniHack tasks.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using predictions from a teacher. This paper examines a problem that can arise when the teacher is especially strong: the student's predictions may differ substantially from the teacher's, and forcing an exact match through KL divergence can disrupt training. The authors report this as an empirical motivation for changing the distillation objective.

Their method, DIST, asks the student to preserve relationships within predictions instead of matching every predicted value exactly. A correlation-based loss captures relationships between classes in the teacher's outputs. The method also matches relationships within each class across different instances, reflecting that examples can have different semantic similarities to that class.

Experiments show that DIST adapts to different architectures, model sizes, and training strategies, with consistently state-of-the-art results reported for image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The findings support relational matching as a practical way to learn from stronger teachers. They show that useful teacher information can be transferred without requiring exact agreement between teacher and student predictions.
neurips-2022-knowledge-distillation-from.tldr: DIST improves distillation from strong teachers by matching prediction relationships through correlation-based losses.

paragraphs: Dynamic view synthesis from monocular video aims to generate new views of changing scenes using a single-camera recording. This paper examines whether existing evaluations reflect practical capture conditions. The authors identify a discrepancy: experimental protocols can effectively supply multi-view signals during training, making their inputs more informative than the monocular framing might suggest.

They introduce effective multi-view factors to quantify these signals through the relative motion of the camera and scene. They also propose co-visibility masked image metrics and correspondence accuracy to address the evaluation issue. A new iPhone dataset adds more diverse real-life deformation sequences, broadening the types of motion used to assess methods.

Under the proposed protocol, state-of-the-art approaches lose 1–2 dB in masked PSNR when multi-view cues are absent and 4–5 dB when modeling complex motion. These results show that capture geometry and motion complexity materially affect measured performance. The paper's contribution is an evaluation framework that makes these dependencies visible and gives a more demanding assessment of monocular dynamic reconstruction.
neurips-2022-monocular-dynamic-view-synt.tldr: A revised evaluation protocol reveals performance drops in monocular dynamic view synthesis when multi-view cues disappear or motion becomes complex.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering organizes nodes using preferences about which nodes should belong together. The objective is to find groups that disagree as little as possible with those preferences. This formulation supports applications such as community detection, duplicate detection, and automated labeling, where the available information describes desired relationships between items.

The paper introduces a simple, computationally efficient algorithm that combines this clustering objective with provable privacy guarantees. Its quality guarantee is expressed through additive error: an allowance for extra disagreement in the clustering objective. This makes the privacy contribution assessable alongside the clustering quality, rather than treating privacy protection as a separate feature with an unspecified effect on the result.

The authors obtain a stronger additive-error guarantee than prior work. For fixed privacy parameters, their error is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. That qualification matters: the result establishes near-optimality at a fixed privacy setting, while retaining a gap expressed by those factors. The stated advance is therefore a theoretically near-optimal privacy-quality guarantee delivered by an efficient algorithm.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-correlation-cl.tldr: An efficient private correlation-clustering algorithm achieves improved additive error that is near-optimal for fixed privacy parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to reach a goal when both action costs and environment transitions can change between episodes. It models the task as a non-stationary stochastic shortest path problem and measures dynamic regret, which accounts for the changing optimal behavior. The aim is to characterize how difficult adaptation is and design algorithms that approach that difficulty limit.

The authors first prove a lower bound involving the number of episodes, state-action pairs, optimal-policy costs and hitting times, and the amounts of cost and transition change. These two kinds of change affect the bound differently, motivating separate estimation of costs and transitions. When their total variation amounts are known, the paper gives a simple suboptimal algorithm and a more involved minimax-optimal algorithm up to logarithmic factors.

The algorithms combine finite-horizon approximation, confidence adjustments, exploration bonuses, and penalties for long-horizon policies. When variation amounts are unknown, a modified MASTER approach provides a separate regret guarantee. This distinguishes near-optimal learning with known change budgets from adaptation without that knowledge.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-goal-oriented-.tldr: New regret bounds and algorithms characterize goal-oriented learning under changing costs and transitions, with near-optimality when change budgets are known.

paragraphs: Many fairness methods seek similar statistical behavior across demographic groups by rescaling classifier scores. This paper starts from the hypothesis that similarities and differences between individuals across groups also matter when measuring unfairness. It develops a way to incorporate that information into the distance between a classifier and predictions that satisfy chosen fairness constraints.

Optimal Transport to Fairness defines unfairness as the smallest transport cost from a probabilistic classifier to any score function meeting those constraints. The construction asks how costly it is to move the existing predictions into an acceptable configuration. Its dependence on transport cost provides a way to account for structure that simple group-level score rescaling can ignore.

For a flexible class of linear fairness constraints, the authors derive a practical differentiable regularizer that can be added to standard classification training. Experiments show that this regularizer can improve the trade-off between predictive power and fairness. The evidence supports this particular constraint-based approach to fairness measurement and optimization, rather than establishing a universal definition of fair prediction.
neurips-2022-optimal-transport-of-classi.tldr: Optimal Transport to Fairness measures the cost of reaching fairness-constrained predictions and can improve the accuracy-fairness trade-off.

paragraphs: Small input perturbations can cause neural networks to make incorrect predictions, and an attack designed for one model may also fool another. This paper studies how normalization layers influence that transferability. It combines empirical evidence with theoretical analysis to motivate a defense built around making attacks transfer poorly between different model configurations.

Random Normalization Aggregation replaces batch normalization layers with a module that aggregates selected normalization types. Each inference samples a random path through these choices, producing a large space of possible configurations. The network can therefore act like an ensemble of many models while drawing a particular configuration for each prediction.

The intended protection comes from designing that random space to have low adversarial transferability. An attack effective against one configuration may have less success against another sampled configuration. The authors argue that this makes effective attacks difficult even when model parameters are accessible, and report strong experimental performance across multiple models and datasets. These findings support the defense empirically without establishing that every possible attack must fail.
neurips-2022-random-normalization-aggreg.tldr: Random Normalization Aggregation strengthens adversarial defense by sampling normalization configurations designed to have low attack transferability.

paragraphs: Training data from external sources may contain poisoned examples that introduce a backdoor into a model. This paper studies detection under limited prior knowledge: the user does not know whether poisoning occurred, which class is targeted, or what fraction of examples was poisoned. The setting also excludes a clean sample set from the training distribution and a trusted model trained on such data.

The method builds on observed differences between channel-level statistics for backdoor triggers and clean image features. Progressive channel shuffling can distinguish their behavior. The proposed randomized channel shuffling procedure uses this effect to detect backdoor-targeted classes with only a few feed-forward passes, keeping computational overhead low.

The authors additionally explore a setting where neither target-class detection nor trigger recovery uses clean data. Experiments span three datasets, three architectures, and three attacks, reporting AUROC improvements of 0.291–0.640 over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The results support efficient backdoor detection under the stated information constraints across the tested combinations.
neurips-2022-randomized-channel-shufflin.tldr: Randomized channel shuffling detects backdoor-targeted classes with few forward passes and without clean reference data or prior poisoning information.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns concept labels to image regions, but obtaining pixel annotations is expensive. Unsupervised methods avoid that supervision yet can still need labeled target examples to connect their predictions to concept names. This paper seeks segmentation models that inherit the broad vocabulary and zero-shot transfer capabilities of language-image pre-training without requiring pixel labels.

ReCo starts with names for the desired concepts and uses CLIP to retrieve relevant images from an unlabeled collection. It then uses correspondences in image representations to co-segment entities across those retrieved groups. The resulting synthetic segments provide training material for a segmentation model, transferring concept knowledge from CLIP into a spatial prediction task.

The authors report favorable performance relative to conventional unsupervised segmentation methods while retaining nameable predictions and zero-shot transfer. They also demonstrate specialist segmenters for extremely rare objects. The contribution is a pipeline that connects text-driven retrieval, shared visual structure, and synthetic segmentation supervision, making broad concept knowledge useful for localization without manually supplied pixel annotations.
neurips-2022-reco-retrieve-and-co-segmen.tldr: ReCo retrieves images with CLIP and co-segments them to train zero-shot segmentation models without pixel labels.

paragraphs: Equivariance builds a symmetry into a neural network: a transformation of the input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. Convolutional networks provide the familiar translation example. Such constraints can be helpful, but choosing them in advance may restrict a model too much when the task only partly follows the assumed symmetry.

This paper proposes a parameter-efficient construction that makes symmetry adjustable. It can interpolate between a non-equivariant linear product, a strictly equivariant convolution, and a strictly invariant mapping. These alternatives represent different requirements on how outputs respond to transformations, allowing one building block to cover a range of symmetry structures.

The authors also show that backpropagation can learn the amount of equivariance from training data. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 classification, this learning achieves similar or better performance than the best setting found through cross-validation and outperforms the compared partial- and strict-equivariance baselines. The findings support treating symmetry strength as something to learn alongside model parameters when a fixed architectural choice may be too restrictive.
neurips-2022-relaxing-equivariance-const.tldr: A parameter-efficient neural building block learns how strongly to enforce equivariance and improves or matches symmetry choices selected by cross-validation.

paragraphs: A point cloud represents a three-dimensional object through a collection of points, but the object also has a compositional organization. Simple parts combine into more complex shapes, which together form the whole. This paper focuses on making that part-whole hierarchy explicit in the features used by a point cloud classifier.

The authors embed classifier features in hyperbolic space and regularize that space to reflect the hierarchy. The geometric choice follows their view that the tree-like organization of parts calls for a representation suited to such structure. Regularization adds an explicit requirement that the learned representation account for composition, connecting the feature space to how object parts are organized.

The paper reports substantial improvements in state-of-the-art supervised point cloud classification models. The stated findings support the usefulness of encoding part-whole structure within the representation used for classification. The contribution lies in coupling a geometric embedding with a hierarchy-aware training constraint, so that compositional information becomes part of how the classifier organizes its features.
neurips-2022-rethinking-the-compositiona.tldr: Embedding and regularizing point cloud features in hyperbolic space to represent part-whole hierarchies improves supervised classification.

paragraphs: Neural posterior estimation uses simulations to infer model parameters from observations. This paper examines what happens when the simulator does not faithfully describe the process that generated those observations. Tests using data produced by the simulator itself address a well-specified setting, leaving the simulation-to-reality gap outside their evaluation.

The authors find that naïvely applying neural posterior estimation under misspecification can produce unreliable inference. They propose addressing two needs together: model criticism that helps identify discrepancies interpretably, and robust inference that can still fit an imperfect but useful simulator. Robust neural posterior estimation explicitly models differences between simulations and observed data to support both aims.

Evaluation on a range of artificially misspecified examples finds that the robust method performs well, while naïve neural posterior estimation produces misleading and erratic posteriors. These findings support making simulator mismatch part of the inference model. The approach treats discrepancy as information to examine and accommodate, helping connect parameter estimation with scrutiny of whether the simulator adequately represents the observations.
neurips-2022-robust-neural-posterior-est.tldr: Robust neural posterior estimation models simulation-observation discrepancies to improve inference and identify misspecification in imperfect simulators.

paragraphs: Point cloud completion reconstructs an object from an incomplete collection of three-dimensional points. This paper introduces SPoVT, a Semantic-Prototype Variational Transformer that uses both the partial geometry and semantic labels attached to the input. Those labels are a stated part of the method's input, giving completion access to information about what the observed points represent.

The model attends to geometric and semantic information to derive point cloud features and semantic prototypes for completion. This ties reconstruction to the semantic organization of the object. The resulting representation supports completing point clouds at varying resolutions and manipulating different semantic parts of an object, making part-level information relevant to both reconstruction and control.

Experiments on benchmark datasets provide quantitative and qualitative evidence for the model's effectiveness and practicality. The stated contribution is therefore broader than predicting missing points alone: it brings semantic information into the completion process and supports operations on meaningful object parts. Its capabilities are presented in the setting where both partial points and their semantic labels are available.
neurips-2022-spovt-semantic-prototype-va.tldr: SPoVT combines partial point clouds with semantic labels to complete objects at varying resolutions and enable semantic-part manipulation.

paragraphs: Branch-and-cut combines branch-and-bound with cutting planes and forms the core of modern integer programming solvers. Choosing which cuts to add is an important part of making these solvers effective. This paper studies the theoretical foundations of learning that choice, focusing on how changes in cut parameters affect the solver's behavior.

The authors develop a structural analysis that tracks the effect of those parameter changes on every step of branch-and-cut. Their argument uses the algorithm's geometric and combinatorial structure. Understanding this dependence provides a basis for reasoning about how a cut-selection rule learned from examples can generalize beyond the examples used to choose it.

The main application is a set of sample complexity guarantees for learning which cutting planes to apply. These guarantees cover infinite cut families, including Gomory mixed integer cuts, which the abstract identifies as central to major solver speedups. The contribution strengthens generalization theory for branch-and-cut by handling a practically important class of choices that cannot be represented merely as a fixed finite list.
neurips-2022-structural-analysis-of-bran.tldr: A structural analysis of branch-and-cut yields sample complexity guarantees for learning cut selection over infinite families, including Gomory mixed integer cuts.

paragraphs: Some high-dimensional inference problems appear computationally difficult even when useful information is present in the data. Researchers study this difficulty through different frameworks, including limits on low-degree functions and statistical-physics descriptions of free-energy landscapes. This paper builds a rigorous connection between those approaches, which otherwise describe computational obstacles in quite different terms.

The authors define a free-energy-based hardness criterion and relate it formally to low-degree hardness. Their connection applies to all Gaussian additive models and certain models containing a sparse planted signal. This scope is central: the theory links the criteria within these classes rather than asserting that every statistical problem has the same relationship.

For Gaussian additive models, the results show that low-degree hardness implies failure of local MCMC algorithms. The connection also provides new low-degree lower bounds for sparse linear regression that seem difficult to obtain directly. The contribution combines a conceptual link between algebraic and geometric views of hardness with concrete tools for proving restrictions on particular computational approaches.
neurips-2022-the-franz-parisi-criterion-.tldr: A free-energy hardness criterion connects low-degree lower bounds with local MCMC failure and yields new bounds for sparse linear regression.

paragraphs: Large recommendation models devote much of their memory to embedding tables. The DLRM benchmark considered here uses 100GB of embedding memory, creating obstacles for training, inference, and deployment. This paper studies a generic parameter-sharing setup that compresses those tables and examines the consequences for both prediction quality and computation.

The authors derive upper bounds on the learnable memory needed to approximate an embedding table. These bounds indicate that exponentially fewer parameters can suffice for a good approximation. Experimentally, their parameter-sharing DLRM achieves 10,000-fold compression on Criteo-tb without losing quality, but reaching the same saturation quality requires 4.5 times as many training iterations.

The smaller model also delivers a 4.3-fold improvement in training latency, producing similar overall training times despite slower convergence in iteration count. The authors report faster inference and easier deployment as additional benefits. The findings show why compression should be evaluated through both optimization and system behavior: more iterations can be offset by making each iteration substantially cheaper.
neurips-2022-the-trade-offs-of-model-siz.tldr: Parameter sharing compresses a Criteo-tb DLRM 10,000-fold without quality loss, with cheaper iterations offsetting slower convergence.

paragraphs: VICE learns numerical representations of object concepts from human judgments. Its data come from a triplet odd-one-out task, in which people identify which object differs from the other two. The goal is to turn those behavioral choices into interpretable vectors that capture aspects of how people organize object concepts.

The method uses approximate Bayesian inference to learn sparse, non-negative embeddings. It also estimates uncertainty in the embedding values, and uses those estimates to select dimensions that best explain the data. This connects representation size to uncertainty-aware evidence about which dimensions are useful, rather than treating every learned dimension as equally supported.

The authors derive a PAC learning bound that can estimate generalization performance or provide a sufficient sample size for experimental design. In predicting human odd-one-out choices, VICE matches or exceeds its predecessor, SPoSE. Its representations are also more reproducible across random initializations. Together, these findings support using uncertainty estimates to obtain interpretable embeddings that predict behavior and remain more consistent across repeated fits.
neurips-2022-vice-variational-interpreta.tldr: VICE learns sparse, uncertainty-aware object embeddings from human judgments, improving reproducibility while matching or exceeding SPoSE's predictive performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether additional questions about points near training examples can enable robust learning without assumptions on the data distribution. Its robustness notion requires agreement throughout a perturbation region. The first query type supplies labels of nearby points, but under the uniform distribution these local membership queries do not increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions or their superclasses.

The authors then introduce local equivalence queries. This oracle checks whether a proposed hypothesis agrees with the target concept throughout a local perturbation region and returns a counterexample when agreement fails. It provides information about an entire region through a query, giving the learner a different form of access to errors.

The query radius is decisive. If it is strictly smaller than the adversary's perturbation budget, distribution-free robust learning remains impossible for many concept classes. When the radii match, the authors construct robust empirical risk minimization algorithms and bound their query requirements using online learning guarantees. They sharpen bounds for conjunctions and provide robust algorithms for halfspaces with margins.
neurips-2022-when-are-local-queries-usef.tldr: Local equivalence queries enable distribution-free robust ERM when their radius matches the adversary's budget, while smaller radii leave broad impossibility results.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly uses negative examples drawn from the current minibatch. This paper examines how that practice can bias training gradients because the loss does not decompose into independent sample contributions. The authors formulate a more general objective with infinitely many negative samples associated with each example and show that direct minibatch optimization can produce biased gradients.

Their remedy is Bayesian data augmentation that converts the objective into a decomposable form. The augmented loss defines a joint distribution over model parameters and additional parameters, which the authors optimize with a stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm. This formulation allows standard stochastic optimization without the gradient bias identified for the original objective.

Experiments cover small models, ImageNet self-supervision, and vision-language representation learning, finding gradient bias throughout the tested settings. The proposed method improves previous results and outperforms MoCo-v3 under the same hyperparameter setting with roughly half the minibatch size. It also achieves strong ELEVATER few-shot classification results. These findings support gradient bias as a useful perspective on contrastive learning's dependence on batch size.
neurips-2022-why-do-we-need-large-batchs.tldr: A Bayesian augmentation removes an identified source of contrastive-learning gradient bias and enables strong results with smaller minibatches.
